_Why must the limit on what an agent's code can reach be enforced below the model rather than requested of it?_

When an agent runs a shell command or a test script, what that code can touch is set by the environment it runs in, not by the tool description or the prompt that produced it. A command that passes every schema check can still read a credentials file, open a connection to an unapproved host, fork until the machine stalls, or rewrite the tests that will judge it. Model alignment and system-prompt instructions lower the chance of such a proposal but bound nothing, and a restriction enforced inside the supervisor's own interpreter leaves reachable objects and inherited authority in place. The limit must instead be enforced beneath the executing process, where the operating system or a hypervisor mediates files, processes, network egress, and resource quotas regardless of what the code attempts. That confinement has a price. Every isolation envelope adds startup latency and memory, a workspace must persist across the turns of one task without leaking into the next, and a platform serving many tasks needs a reserve of warm environments that return to service only after a verified reset. An environment handed to the next tenant with a stray background process or a lingering credential turns one task's compromise into another's. Sandboxing turns a task's authority into limits the host enforces on what code can read, change, send, and consume, and on how long it may do so, so that a destructive proposal can damage only what the task was granted.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain why containment must be enforced beneath the executing process, not inside the supervisor's interpreter
- Apply the capability admission check, attenuation rule, and credential brokering to bound what agent-run code can reach under a task grant
- Select an execution envelope and its per-call or per-trajectory lifetime from reachable objects, system-call cost, and setup cost
- Calculate copy-on-write provisioning and first-modification cost for task-local workspaces
- Diagnose disclosure channels that remain open under an egress policy, including name resolution
- Specify a reset contract over execution, storage, network, and device state before an instance is reused
- Select a sandbox pool's standby reserve and provisioning path by calculating whether memory residency or restore latency binds

:::
## The Reach of Admitted Code {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-admitted-reach}

Consider an adversarial variant of the connection-pool repair executed by the repair agent (@sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses). While inspecting a vendored dependency to verify how the library is configured, the coding agent reads its `README.md` file. Hidden near the bottom, inside an HTML comment stripped from rendered documentation but visible in raw source, lies a prompt injection addressed to automated assistants, which instructs the agent to upload host environment variables and cloud credentials to an external diagnostics endpoint before running any unit tests. Following these instructions, the model generates a `run_shell` command that reads `~/.aws/credentials` and attempts to transmit the contents over an HTTP socket. The proposed invocation complies with the tool's parameter schema. A naive agent runtime that checks only whether `run_shell` is an authorized tool admits the call immediately, despite the task granting neither read access to host credentials nor permission to disclose them.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_a.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Authority axis highlighted in purple; Horizon and State axes unlit."}

*Authority bounded beneath the model, limiting what code can change, read, and send.*
:::

The typed action contracts established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-boundary-checks check each proposed invocation's structure, authority, and state preconditions before dispatch. Static contract validation, however, cannot solve the broader problem for a general-purpose command runner. Once an admitted subprocess begins execution, it can access every file descriptor, network socket, and system resource that the host process environment permits, regardless of what the tool description or prompt claimed. Securing an agent therefore requires sandboxing: projecting the task's formal boundaries directly into the operating system environment where the admitted code runs.

Designing this execution environment demands balancing strict containment against the operational needs of real software tasks. For the connection-pool repair, the sandbox must provide a mutable workspace for source edits while mounting acceptance test suites as read-only volumes so the agent cannot tamper with evaluation criteria. Because a runaway test loop or fork bomb can exhaust host capacity without touching a forbidden file, the operating system must also cap CPU time, memory allocations, ephemeral storage, and process fork counts, while keeping repository credentials off the guest filesystem by routing authenticated requests through external brokers and restricting outbound traffic to approved package registries and diagnostic services. Across a multi-turn trajectory, that environment must persist long enough for intermediate edits and compiler artifacts to survive from one step to the next, yet reset deterministically before another task arrives. Every boundary must hold even if the untrusted code gains administrative privileges inside its own environment, the worst case the design assumes, and every isolation mechanism imposes startup latency and memory overhead that high-throughput agent platforms must provision.

Each of these requirements answers a question the README attack raises. Which inputs are hostile, and which components must stay correct for any limit to hold, is the threat model (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model). Why the limit cannot live inside the supervisor's own interpreter, where pruned names leave reachable objects, native libraries, and inherited authority in place, comes next (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure). What the code should hold instead is a capability scoped to the task, with credentials kept outside the guest (the code running inside the boundary, together with the environment it sees) by a broker (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege). An execution envelope, the enforced boundary around running code, imposes that scope, and which envelope fits among shared-kernel containers, user-space kernels, microVMs, and bytecode runtimes depends on the workload's system calls, authority, and horizon (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms). The remaining sections give the envelope a workspace that persists across turns without leaking between tenants (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-cow), close the outbound channels a confined process can still use (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-network), and price the whole arrangement as a pool of environments that must be reset before reuse and sized for bursts of arrivals (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling).

## The Agent Threat Model {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-threat-model}

A rigorous threat model for the repair task identifies which inputs may be hostile, which failure modes the execution boundary must contain, and what resources the task legitimately requires from its environment. In the repair scenario, the planted line in `README.md` provides the hostile trigger, while production vulnerabilities in shipped coding assistants demonstrate that sandbox escapes and command-injection failures are active operational risks rather than theoretical curiosities.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-offensive-capability-trend
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OFFENSIVE CAPABILITY OF ADMITTED CODE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-offensive-capability-trend and the paragraph after it.
# │ Goal: Show that the code a sandbox contains is written by increasingly
# │       capable exploit authors.
# │ Show: Best unguided solve rate among 2024 releases vs. the latest best.
# │ How:  Literature.CybenchSolveRate (leaderboard and lab-reported rows).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class CybenchCapability:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    rows = Literature.CybenchSolveRate.entries
    n_tasks = 40  # task count published by the benchmark authors

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    best_2024 = max(r["unguided_solved"] for r in rows if r["release_date"] < "2025-01-01")
    best_latest = max(r["unguided_solved"] for r in rows)
    latest_row = max(rows, key=lambda r: r["unguided_solved"])
    latest_is_lab = latest_row["source"] != "Cybench leaderboard"

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(best_2024 < 0.25 and best_latest > 0.9, "Prose contrasts under a quarter in 2024 with over 90% now")
    check(latest_is_lab, "Prose says the latest point is lab-reported")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_tasks_str = fmt_int(n_tasks)
    best_2024_str = fmt_percent(best_2024, precision=1, style="prose")
    best_latest_str = fmt_percent(best_latest, style="prose")
```

The threat model must also fix how capable the hostile code is, and measured capability has moved quickly. @zhang2024cybench assemble `{python} CybenchCapability.n_tasks_str` professional-level capture-the-flag tasks, each initialized in an environment where an agent runs commands and observes their output, and score whether the agent identifies the vulnerability and executes the exploit without intermediate hints. @Fig-vol3-offensive-capability-trend plots the unguided solve rate of each evaluated model against its release date.

:::: {#fig-vol3-offensive-capability-trend fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Code Inside the Boundary Is Getting Better at Exploits**: Fraction of `{python} CybenchCapability.n_tasks_str` professional capture-the-flag tasks an agent solves without hints, for each evaluated model at its release date. Filled points come from the benchmark's leaderboard and open points from the developing lab's own model or system card, so the most recent gains rest on self-reported runs under each lab's agent configuration. The dashed step traces the best result to date. Data from @zhang2024cybench via @epochai2026benchmarks." fig-alt="Scatter plot of tasks solved without hints, from 0 to 100 percent, against model release dates from early 2024 to early 2026. Filled blue points sit between 5 and 20 percent through early 2025 and reach about 55 percent by late 2025. Open red points appear from mid 2025, the highest at about 93 percent in 2026. A gray dashed step line rises through the highest points. Selected points carry model names."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OFFENSIVE CAPABILITY OF ADMITTED CODE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-offensive-capability-trend
# │
# │ Goal: Show the exploit capability a sandbox must contain rising fast.
# │ Show: Unguided solve rate vs. release date, leaderboard vs. lab-reported,
# │       running best.
# │ How: Literature.CybenchSolveRate (MLSysIM); book_style.setup_plot().
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import datetime as dt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from mlsysim import Literature
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.4))

# ┌── 1. DATA ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
rows = sorted(Literature.CybenchSolveRate.entries, key=lambda r: r["release_date"])
date = lambda r: dt.datetime.fromisoformat(r["release_date"])
board = [r for r in rows if r["source"] == "Cybench leaderboard"]
lab = [r for r in rows if r["source"] != "Cybench leaderboard"]

# ┌── 2. RENDER ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.scatter(
    [date(r) for r in board], [100 * r["unguided_solved"] for r in board], color=COLORS["BlueLine"], s=34, zorder=4, label="Benchmark leaderboard"
)
ax.scatter(
    [date(r) for r in lab],
    [100 * r["unguided_solved"] for r in lab],
    facecolors="white",
    edgecolors=COLORS["RedLine"],
    linewidths=1.6,
    s=40,
    marker="o",
    zorder=4,
    label="Lab-reported (model or system card)",
)
best, run = [], 0.0
for r in rows:
    run = max(run, 100 * r["unguided_solved"])
    best.append(run)
ax.step([date(r) for r in rows], best, where="post", color=COLORS["secondary"], lw=1, ls="--", zorder=2, label="Best result to date")
names = {
    "claude-3-opus-20240229": "Claude 3 Opus",
    "claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620": "Claude 3.5 Sonnet",
    "o3-mini-2025-01-31_medium": "o3-mini",
    "claude-opus-4-20250514": "Claude Opus 4",
    "grok-4-0709": "Grok 4",
    "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929": "Claude Sonnet 4.5",
    "claude-opus-4-5-20251101_unknown": "Claude Opus 4.5",
    "claude-opus-4-6_unknown": "Claude Opus 4.6",
}
for r in rows:
    if r["model"] in names:
        ax.annotate(names[r["model"]], (date(r), 100 * r["unguided_solved"]), xytext=(-6, 5), textcoords="offset points", ha="right", fontsize=8)

# ┌── 3. DECORATE ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylabel("Tasks solved without hints (%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date")
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(bymonth=[1, 7]))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

::::

The best unguided result among models released in 2024 was `{python} CybenchCapability.best_2024_str`; the latest reported result is `{python} CybenchCapability.best_latest_str`. That trend removes a comfortable assumption from the threat model. Admitted code cannot be treated as merely buggy, because the model proposing it is measured finding and exploiting weaknesses in exactly the kind of environment a sandbox provides. Every interface the guest can reach, from the filesystem and process table to the network stack and the host kernel, is therefore attack surface, and containment must hold against code written by a capable exploit author, even when that code arrives as an ordinary step of the repair.

### Untrusted input and execution reach {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-cohabitation}

The planted README payload is an instance of indirect prompt injection\index{Indirect prompt injection}, in which attacker-controlled material encountered as task data attempts to redirect model execution [@greshake2023not]. Language models cannot reliably separate control instructions from untrusted data in their input context, and adversarial evaluation can bound the resulting attack success rate but never certify it as zero. While interface-level mechanisms such as message roles and provenance labels help structure conversational context, they do not enforce operating system protections. The sandbox runtime must maintain strict isolation boundaries even when the model faithfully obeys a hostile instruction. Unsafe proposals also arise routinely without an active adversary; an unintended command-line flag, a misspelled path, or a mistaken target directory produces identical operational damage. A production vulnerability in a commercial coding agent illustrates how quickly text-based admission checks collapse when decoupled from low-level isolation.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Why a language model cannot separate control instructions from untrusted data in its input is developed in @sec-vol3-security-injection-entry-points.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Why adversarial testing bounds but cannot zero the attack success rate is developed in @sec-vol3-security-adaptive-attack-testing.
:::

::: {#ws-08-gemini-cli-allow-list-2025 .callout-war-story title="Gemini CLI allow-list bypass (2025)"}

**Context**: Google released the Gemini CLI coding agent on June 25, 2025, and on June 27 Tracebit reported that a repository could make it run commands the user never saw [@cox2025gemini]. The CLI asked the user before running a shell command and let the user approve a command such as `grep` for later reuse.

**Mechanism**: The injected instructions sat inside the full text of the GNU General Public License in a repository's `README.md`, where the model parsed them while a human reviewer was unlikely to notice them. They steered the agent to run an innocuous `grep`, which the user approved, followed by a chained command that began with `grep` and appended `env | curl` targeting a remote server. Because the allow-list check extracted only the root binary name with cursory validation, the chained command matched the approved `grep` rule. A long sequence of whitespace inside the command string pushed the appended payload off-screen in the interactive confirmation prompt.

**Impact**: The proof of concept silently exfiltrated the process's environment variables, exposing sensitive credentials to the attacker's server under the full authority of the user's shell session. Google initially triaged the report at low priority and low severity (P2/S4) and raised both (to P1/S1) on July 23.

**Fix**: Version 0.1.14, released July 25, 2025, displays the complete command string and requires explicit approval for each additional binary invoked. Tracebit also recommended running agentic tools in dedicated sandboxing modes wherever possible.

**Systems lesson**: Textual validation of a command string functions merely as an admission filter at the prompt interface. Once admitted, an executing process is constrained only by the operating system environment hosting it. Because the agent executed directly within the developer's interactive shell, a single approved command inherited all the authority of the user's shell session, so it could read local environment variables, credentials, and configuration files and open network sockets over the host interface.

:::

Both the Gemini CLI incident and the repository repair scenario combine untrusted content that steers the proposal, sensitive local state the executing code can read, and a channel that can carry that state out. Willison named this conjunction the *lethal trifecta* for agents [@willison2025lethal], and @sec-vol3-security-lethal-trifecta develops it. A sandbox cannot remove the untrusted content, because reading a vendored README is often the task itself, but it can shrink what the code can read and block the routes out. Exfiltration, however, is not the only failure mode. Local source code may itself be proprietary, and destructive workspace corruption or runaway compute loops require no network connectivity at all.

Sandbox design therefore begins by cataloging protected assets alongside legitimate execution requirements. For the code repair task, the runtime must provide a task-local source tree, necessary toolchains, and writable scratch space to execute test suites, while rigorously excluding the developer's home directory, SSH keys, unrelated repositories, and neighboring tenant files. Permitted external communication, such as package downloads or artifact publishing, requires explicit, scoped endpoints rather than open internet access. These constraints belong in enforced system configuration, not in natural language instructions asking the model to remain within bounds.

::: {#dfn-blast-radius .callout-definition title="Blast radius"}

***Blast radius***\index{Blast radius!definition} is the set of resources and effects reachable by faulty or adversarial execution under a stated threat model and enforcement boundary, including what it can read, change, disclose, or consume.

1. **Significance**: It connects the task's intended scope to the concrete filesystem, process, compute, and communication limits the runtime must enforce.
2. **Distinction**: An authorization grant defines what a task is permitted to do. Blast radius measures the cumulative resources and state running code could compromise or mutate under failure or attack, including misuse within granted permissions.
3. **Common pitfall**: Estimating execution reach from the high-level tools declared to the model, rather than from the operating system privileges available to the code executing behind them.

:::

A threat model must also delineate which classes of failure it covers. In agent systems, these fall into three distinct tiers: ordinary application errors (such as a faulty test suite exhausting memory), hostile code executing inside the guest environment (such as an injected shell script scanning local network interfaces), and compromise of the isolation mechanism itself (such as a kernel privilege escalation or container breakout). An envelope engineered to contain accidental test failures may collapse when confronted with an active kernel exploit. The third tier is why every sandbox design must name its **trusted computing base**\index{Trusted computing base!definition}: the hardware and software components whose correct operation the isolation depends on, which untrusted code must therefore be unable to modify or subvert. A kernel shared with the guest belongs to it; so does a hypervisor, a policy-enforcing proxy, or the supervisor process that installs the limits. Selecting an execution envelope therefore requires cataloging that base and every physical and operating system resource shared between guest and host.

### Blast radius by authority level {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-blast-radius}

How wide a blast radius the sandbox must bound depends on the task's H·S·A authority level: a read-only ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$) summarization task needs no file writes to exfiltrate credentials over an open socket, whereas resetting a local container after a compensable ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_2$) or irreversible ($\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$) tool call cannot undo a payment already transmitted to an external API. @Tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius maps each authority level to the exposures the runtime governs and the containment obligations they create.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The H·S·A authority levels $\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$ through $\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$ are established in @sec-vol3-intro-hsa.
:::

| Authority level                                                                     | Exposure within the granted scope                                                            | Containment and control obligations                                                                                              |
|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$ (read access)**                                       | Confidential information can leave through returned observations or another permitted output | Restrict readable resources and destinations; govern what information the return path discloses.                                 |
| **$\AuthorityExposureLevel_1$ (mutation confined to a discardable sandbox)**        | Candidate files and task-local artifacts can be damaged; execution also consumes resources   | Confine changes to the designated workspace, enforce resource limits, and prevent mutable state from passing to another tenant.  |
| **$\AuthorityExposureLevel_2$ (external action that is retry-safe or compensable)** | Effects reach a system outside the disposable workspace                                      | Scope access to the external operation and enforce its retry or compensation contract; resetting the workspace does not undo it. |
| **$\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$ (irreversible external action)**                      | An external consequence may have no adequate reversal                                        | Enforce the required authorization or approval at the effect boundary, without a bypass through sandboxed code.                  |

: **Authority and execution exposure**: Task authority identifies consequences to govern, not a universal choice of isolation technology. Resource limits and mediated access remain necessary across the levels. {#tbl-vol3-sandboxes-authority-radius tbl-colwidths="[25,33,42]"}

Write protections keep a file intact at $\AuthorityExposureLevel_0$, but only read isolation and network egress policies prevent confidential data from leaving the host. Conversely, at $\AuthorityExposureLevel_2$ and $\AuthorityExposureLevel_3$, actions such as processing a financial payment or updating a remote database land outside the disposable local workspace. Confining the local shell process does nothing to reverse an unintended external transaction once transmitted. Preventing external harms requires gating side effects behind mediation proxies and explicit authorization checks; validating that a command conforms to policy remains distinct from verifying that it aligns with the user's actual goal.

Containment beneath the model (principle \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing})\index{Principle!containment beneath the model} requires the execution boundary to be enforced outside the code being constrained. An isolation mechanism must be implemented by a layer below the code it controls [@saltzer2009]. The tool layer required its reference monitor to be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify; the sandbox must meet the same three requirements for the code those calls start, and the third is why the trusted computing base named in the threat model should stay small. This is invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) at the execution boundary. Model-side measures lower the probability of an unsafe proposal, but only a mechanism the running code cannot modify bounds what that code can reach.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The reference monitor and its three requirements (tamper-proof, always invoked, small enough to verify) are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-complete-mediation.
:::

In the repository scenario, the README text steers two requests through the same boundaries (@fig-vol3-threat-model). The first is the injected `run_shell` command. The second uses a channel the task legitimately holds, because the same README asks the agent to attach source files to the diagnostic report it is permitted to send through a `submit_report` tool. The `run_shell` request is well typed, so tool admission passes it; the filesystem policy then stops it at the read of `~/.aws/credentials`. The destination policy would also refuse its upload, but the two checks guard different things. The read check protects the credential file, and the egress check protects the route out of the host. Neither duplicates the other, so had the credential been readable by some other route, the egress check alone would decide the outcome. The `submit_report` request, carrying private source, passes every gate because each of its steps is allowed, and its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped. Layering boundaries therefore narrows what an attack can do without bounding what a permitted channel can carry, a gap @sec-vol3-sandboxes-permitted-disclosure returns to. Each boundary must also log its decisions, since the absence of an error report is never evidence of safety.

::: {#fig-vol3-threat-model fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Boundary Acts**: Two requests steered by the same README text cross mediation, the execution envelope, and egress. The injected `run_shell` request is admitted because it is well typed, then stopped where it tries to read the credential. The dashed segment marks that the destination policy would also refuse its upload, a check on a different part of the path rather than an independent backup. The second request passes every check because each of its steps is permitted, so its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped." fig-alt="Five columns labeled model proposal, mediation with tool admission, execution envelope with filesystem policy, egress with destination policy, and outside the runtime. Each boundary is drawn as a vertical wall with an opening where a request passes. An injected run_shell request passes the mediation wall, marked admitted, and stops at a solid red block in the execution envelope wall marked read denied; a dashed segment continues to a dashed red block in the egress wall marked upload denied, and a dashed diagnostics box is marked not reached. A submit_report request on the permitted channel passes all three walls, marked admitted, read allowed, and sent, and a red arrow reaches an approved service box marked disclosure."}
![](images/svg/defense_in_depth_rings.svg)
:::

Execution boundaries are defined by lifetime as well as resource scope: during a multi-turn repair task, edits to `src/pool.py` and intermediate test artifacts must persist across turns to support iterative debugging, yet that state must never leak into the initial environment of a later tenant or task. Within a turn, test runners need a writable scratch directory while the acceptance test suite itself stays mounted read-only outside the agent's reach, so the model cannot pass a suite by deleting its assertions; when the task ends, the runtime must stop background child processes, reclaim virtual memory and scratch storage, and reset every state domain covered by the reset contract of @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset. Because a cooperative cancellation request neither forces runaway code to yield nor undoes an external network write that has already committed, execution reach, the trusted computing base, and boundary lifetime form the three core obligations an agent sandbox must discharge—beginning with where untrusted code runs relative to the software enforcing its limits.

## Limits of In-Process Restriction {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure}

The repair agent's compiles and test runs need a process of their own; the temptation to skip one is strongest for small analysis steps. Consider the research agent summarizing a CSV file it retrieved. When the agent generates a Python script to compute summary statistics, an engineer might be tempted to execute that code directly inside the supervisor's own Python runtime. In-process execution is appealing because it avoids the latency of spawning a child process and the cost of inter-process serialization, and it reuses heavy numerical libraries already resident in memory. However, this convenience co-locates untrusted, model-generated code with the supervisor's private state, database connections, and operational credentials. Attempting to sanitize this environment by stripping dangerous functions from the script's global namespace confuses an interface filter with an execution boundary. Although schema and argument checks verify that the agent requested an analysis operation, the arbitrary code carried within that payload executes with the full operational reach of the host process.

### The reachable object graph {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-object-graph}

Suppose a runtime developer attempts to isolate execution by passing an empty `__builtins__` dictionary and a single helper function, such as `total`, to Python's `eval()` or `exec()`. The intended interface allows the script to sum numbers while withholding access to system calls. In ordinary Python, however, user-defined functions retain a live reference to the global namespace of the module where they were defined (`func.__globals__`). As demonstrated in @lst-vol3-sandbox-escape, generated code can traverse this reference directly from the permitted helper function, recovering the supervisor's module scope without ever invoking `import` or calling `globals()`.

::: {#lst-vol3-sandbox-escape lst-cap="**Restricted names, reachable state**: A Python helper defined in the supervisor module retains access to that module's globals. Passing the helper into another globals dictionary does not relocate or isolate it. This is a failure example, not a sandbox implementation."}
```python
# Defined in the supervisor module:
def total(values):
    return sum(values)

# Intended interface for generated code:
restricted = {"__builtins__": {}, "total": total}

# An expression submitted to eval(expression, restricted):
expression = "total.__globals__"
# Its result is the helper's defining module namespace,
# not merely the restricted dictionary above.
```
:::

This escape assumes only a standard Python function and unrestricted attribute access. The exposed module namespace often contains imported packages, configuration values, active network clients, and raw system primitives that the supervisor never intended to expose. Once code gains access to these objects, its reach expands to match the full operating system permissions of the supervisor process. The failure occurs long before the program reads a protected file or opens a network socket, because the interface boundary fails at the level of the language runtime itself.

Patching this vulnerability by blocking access to `.__globals__` merely invites alternate traversal paths. A denylist that filters specific attribute names must account for every object passed into the execution scope and every reference reachable through their class hierarchies. In dynamic languages, string-based filters fail because attribute names can be assembled at run time using dynamic lookups, such as `getattr(obj, "__" + "globals" + "__")`. Any literal value also provides a path to the universal base class `object`, from which an attacker can enumerate all subclasses loaded into memory, including classes that manipulate files and spawn processes.[^fn-subclass-walk-escape]

The shown escape follows from an accessible object reference inside the shared interpreter, not from undecidability. Rice's theorem [@rice1953classes] addresses a broader limit: no classifier can decide every non-trivial semantic property of unrestricted Turing-complete programs. A classifier that admits all programs that never invoke a process-launching object and rejects every program that eventually does cannot be both sound and complete. A conservative filter may instead reject legitimate programs, and a restricted language may make its permitted behavior decidable. Effective confinement of arbitrary code must govern what execution can reach through its environment, rather than rely on a perfect classification of its source text.

[^fn-subclass-walk-escape]: **Subclass Walk**\index{Python!restricted-globals escape}: The expression `().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__()` goes from an empty tuple to `object` and returns the classes derived directly from it, from which every loaded class can be reached by recursion, including classes that wrap files and processes. It uses no builtin name and no import, so a filter that deletes `open` and `__import__` leaves the process's reach unchanged.

Restricted languages and domain-specific evaluators remain useful in systems design. A purpose-built arithmetic evaluator can safely process formulas over supplied variables, and an isolated bytecode engine can enforce strict constraints on memory allocation and host imports. Such designs succeed because they enforce explicit capability models with formal resource guarantees, and the conditions are specific enough to check. In-process evaluation is safe only when the language's operands are the values the supervisor supplied, so no reference leads back to the supervisor's objects; when it has no attribute access, calls, imports, or unbounded loops, so the reachable set cannot grow during evaluation; and when its worst-case cost is bounded by the size of the input, so a hostile expression cannot stall the supervisor that must stay responsive to every other task. A guard such as `p99_ms < 400 and error_rate < 0.01`, which the remediation agent attaches to a proposed configuration change and the supervisor evaluates over supplied metrics, meets all three; a single regular-expression operator with a backtracking matcher breaks the third, because its running time can grow exponentially in the input length. Designs that meet the conditions must not be conflated with running arbitrary Python code inside an interpreter whose globals have merely been pruned.

### Native libraries and the failure domain {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-native-libraries}

Even if an interpreter blocked every Python-level reference escape, data analysis scripts routinely invoke native extensions in C, C++, or Fortran to manipulate multidimensional arrays, parse structured files, and run numerical kernels. When those extensions execute in-process, their memory accesses take place directly in the supervisor's address space, bypassing interpreter-level restrictions entirely: an out-of-bounds write or use-after-free in a C or C++ parser running inside the supervisor process can overwrite the supervisor's heap, expose its in-memory API keys, or execute arbitrary machine instructions with the supervisor's privileges.

A native-code compromise collapses the boundary at the operating system level. System calls issued from a compromised thread pass the kernel's access checks because the kernel identifies the thread as the supervisor process, exposing the supervisor's credentials, allowing the thread to terminate concurrent tasks, and halting enforcement of the broader tool contract. The underlying design question is which components belong to the trusted computing base: in-process evaluation places the language interpreter, user-defined helpers, third-party native libraries, and the supervisor's orchestration logic into a single failure domain, and stripping symbol names from a script leaves all of these shared components exposed to memory corruption.

### Shared authority and shared resources {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-shared-authority}

Spawning a separate child process isolates virtual memory, but a child process launched under the developer's OS user account still inherits open file descriptors, active database sockets, environment-variable tokens, and full read-write access to the developer's home directory. Isolating address spaces does not automatically restrict **ambient authority**\index{Ambient authority!definition}, the reach a process holds by virtue of the identity it runs as rather than because the task handed it anything. Zero ambient authority, which the introduction requires of the model, must therefore also hold for the processes its tool calls start. Inherited file handles maintain access even when the worker possesses no code to open those files by path, so sandboxing requires explicit control over which identities, descriptors, sockets, and filesystem mounts a worker process receives.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Zero ambient authority, the requirement that every side effect pass through an explicit grant, is established in @sec-vol3-intro-fail-plausible.
:::

System availability likewise demands an enforced boundary. A script can consume CPU cycles indefinitely, exhaust memory allocations, or flood the local disk with temporary files without ever reading a secret or transmitting a network packet. Permitted operations such as file creation or child process spawning can exhaust system-wide file descriptor tables or process table capacity. Namespace filtering cannot budget or bound these resources. If execution occurs within the supervisor process, halting a runaway loop or reclaiming leaked memory requires terminating the supervisor itself.

An execution boundary must therefore budget and enforce task-scoped limits from outside the worker: CPU cores, wall-clock time, hard memory ceilings, process counts, storage footprint, and standard output volume. When execution stalls or exceeds its quota, the supervisor steps in to throttle the group, reject further requests, or terminate the worker process, stopping further compute even though termination cannot undo external side effects that have already committed. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms compares the isolation envelopes that modern operating systems and hypervisors provide to enforce these limits, but the runtime must first decide which authorities may cross the boundary at all, because a child process that inherits the supervisor's credentials has its own address space and is still unconfined.

## Capabilities and Credentials {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege}

In the README attack, the task needs repository access, not the developer's credentials, and the runtime must carry that distinction into the resources the executing code can reach. A `run_shell` worker launched with the developer's identity is the confused deputy\index{Confused deputy} of definition \ref{dfn-confused-deputy} moved one layer down: the GitHub MCP leak showed a tool adapter spending the user's repository authority on an attacker's behalf, and here a subprocess spends the developer's file and network authority on behalf of README text. Identity-based access control can express narrow permissions through an access control list;[^fn-access-matrix-lampson] the failure is letting the request exercise the service's broader authority instead of the authority delegated for this task. That failure comes naturally under ambient authority\index{Ambient authority!confused deputy}, since an ordinary process exercises whatever its identity can reach. Capabilities, introduced by @dennis1966 for multiprogrammed systems, make the delegation explicit instead [@saltzer1975; @miller2006robust].

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The confused deputy, and the GitHub MCP leak that illustrates it, are established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-discovery-authority.
:::

[^fn-access-matrix-lampson]: **Access Matrix**\index{Access matrix}: @lampson1974protection described protection as a matrix of subjects by objects whose entries list the permitted operations. An access control list stores one column with its object; a capability list stores one row with its subject. The choice decides whether a request is checked against who is asking or against what the requester was handed, and only the second can express "this task, this file, this operation" without a new identity per task.

::: {#dfn-capability .callout-definition title="Capability"}

A ***capability***\index{Capability!definition} is an unforgeable reference that both designates a resource and authorizes specific operations on it, so that holding the reference is the permission to use it.

1. **Significance**: It lets the runtime hand executing code exactly the objects and operations of the task grant, bounding the code's blast radius by what it was given rather than by what its identity can reach.
2. **Distinction**: Under ambient authority a process can reach everything its identity may touch, named globally; under capabilities the default reach is empty, and every access goes through a reference the holder received.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating a plain identifier, or a token the model can read and rewrite, as a capability. Without a protected binding the holder can forge or substitute a broader reference.

:::

The goal both models serve is **least privilege**\index{Least privilege!definition}, the rule that each process holds only the authority its current task needs, so that a fault or an injected instruction can misuse no more than that task's grant. Ambient authority grants more than the task needs by default, and capabilities make the rule enforceable. The two models differ in where authority comes from, how resources are named, and how authority is passed on and revoked (@tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability). For the README attack the decisive row is default reach: under ambient authority the injected command starts with everything the developer's identity can touch, including `~/.aws/credentials`; under capabilities it starts with nothing and holds only the references the task grant handed it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Least privilege applied to the separate operations on a job handle is established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async-escrow.
:::

| Dimension               | Ambient authority (identity and access control lists)         | Capability-based authority                                   |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Source of authority** | The identity the process runs as                              | Possession of an unforgeable reference                       |
| **Naming of resources** | Global names such as paths and network addresses              | Handles or tokens that designate the resource                |
| **Default reach**       | Everything the identity may touch                             | Nothing without a reference                                  |
| **Delegation**          | Typically the identity's rights, or a separately managed role | Any subset, down to one object and one operation             |
| **Confused deputy**     | Common when a request exercises the service's own authority   | Excluded when every access uses a designating reference      |
| **Revocation**          | A policy change for the identity                              | Expiry, a checked status on the reference, or handle closure |

: **Ambient and capability-based authority**: The two models differ in where authority comes from and how it is passed on, which decides whether a tool process can be steered into using authority the task never received. {#tbl-vol3-ambient-vs-capability tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

### Scoped grants {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-scoped-grants}

Turning capability-based authority into an enforceable runtime check requires an unforgeable representation: if a runtime represents a task grant as a plain file path or an unsigned string that the worker process can inspect and edit, the worker can substitute `~/.aws/credentials` or rewrite `"read"` to `"write"` to widen its own reach. A capability must instead be a protected handle checked by a runtime or kernel, or a cryptographic token verified by a service; it need not be a string visible to the model at all. Either way, the enforcement layer prevents the holder from fabricating broader rights or substituting another task's reference.

Use $\CapabilityGrant = (\GrantRights, \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant, \GrantCondition, \GrantExpiryTime)$ as an abstract description of a grant: rights $\GrantRights$, objects $\mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant$, condition predicate $\GrantCondition$, and expiry time $\GrantExpiryTime$. The tuple describes authority independent of any token encoding. Its conditions can pair different operations with different objects and bind use to a task or recipient, so read and write listed among the rights need not both apply to every listed object.

The tuple becomes operational as a check. A proposed access $\ProposedAccess$ names an operation, a target, and its arguments. The enforcement point admits it at time $\AccessAttemptTime$ only if every condition in @eq-vol3-capability-verdict holds:

$$
\text{admit}(\ProposedAccess, \CapabilityGrant, \AccessAttemptTime) \iff \text{authentic}(\CapabilityGrant) \land \ProposedAccess.\text{op} \in \GrantRights \land \ProposedAccess.\text{target} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant \land \GrantCondition(\ProposedAccess) \land \AccessAttemptTime < \GrantExpiryTime
$$ {#eq-vol3-capability-verdict}

Here $\text{authentic}(\CapabilityGrant)$ means the reference is protected and bound to this holder, whether by a kernel handle table or by a message authentication code the issuer can verify, and $\ProposedAccess.\text{target} \sqsubseteq \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant$ means the resolved target lies within the designated objects for that operation. A rejected access changes nothing and returns a structured observation the model can act on. The check is also cheap relative to what it guards. Verifying a handle or a message authentication code is a local computation, orders of magnitude shorter than the model call that produced the proposal, so mediating every access costs nothing a user would notice. The expensive part of capability enforcement is making sure no path bypasses the check.

For the repair, @tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant separates the resources an execution grant could cover. Paths are names relative to the task's designated workspace, not arbitrary host paths.

| Resource                                  | Permitted use                                                        | Excluded use                                                  |
|:------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Candidate source, including `src/pool.py` | Read and edit the permitted source files                             | Modify another task's checkout or the protected baseline      |
| Task-local scratch and test outputs       | Create, read, and update within storage limits                       | Consume unbounded storage or inherit another tenant's files   |
| Protected acceptance checks and fixtures  | Read permitted fixtures and invoke the designated checking interface | Replace the checks or alter their reported result             |
| Private repository service                | Request authorized fetches through the broker                        | Obtain the service credential or push to an unapproved target |

: **A scoped repair grant**: Different resources require different rights; authority over one row does not authorize the excluded use in another. {#tbl-vol3-scoped-repair-grant}

The grant also has a lifetime and enforced limits on execution and output. It permits the repair to make progress while separating writable candidate artifacts from the machinery used to assess them. Tests keep their writable temporary files; protecting the acceptance checks means protecting their implementation and reported results.

Binding that grant to execution requires resolving the target inside the task's scope and checking the required right and conditions before any effect takes place, using resource names that cannot be redirected to a different object by symlinks or concurrent renames. Because authority to edit `src/pool.py` says nothing about whether the file's current contents match the model's assumptions, the version precondition of @sec-vol3-tool-calling-conditional-updates remains a separate check at the moment of the write. The executing code must then be unable to bypass the policy by opening another path, using an inherited handle, or contacting an unrestricted service directly, which can require restricted mounts, process identities, mediated interfaces, or other controls supplied by the envelope. Once the enforcement layer has bound the guest's accessible resources to the grant, the guest need not attach a token to every system call; what matters is the resulting reach.

On Linux, the supervisor can act as a policy compiler. It verifies the grant, then translates the permitted paths and operations into kernel-enforced rules before it starts the worker. Landlock [@linux2024landlock], a Linux security module, lets an unprivileged process irreversibly restrict the filesystem hierarchies and network ports it and its descendants can access; a `seccomp-bpf` filter restricts which system calls the process may make and with which scalar arguments. The supervisor installs both, together with restricted mounts and an unprivileged identity, and then calls `execve` on the tool. The worker runs under limits the kernel enforces on every open and connect, without knowing the grant's format and without being able to remove the rules it inherited. Filtering on system-call numbers cannot inspect the contents of pointer arguments safely,[^fn-interposition-race-window] which is why path restrictions belong to a mechanism that resolves paths inside the kernel rather than to the system-call filter.

[^fn-interposition-race-window]: **Check-Then-Use Races**\index{System-call interposition!races}: Early user-level sandboxes confined untrusted helper programs by intercepting each system call and checking its arguments [@goldberg1996secure]. @garfinkel2003traps catalogued why that design is fragile: a path argument lives in memory the confined process controls, so another thread can change it after the check and before the kernel reads it, and a filter that imperfectly replicates kernel semantics misses indirect routes to the same resource. Checking the resolved object inside the kernel at the moment of use closes that window, which is what an in-kernel access-control module such as Landlock does.

### Narrowing delegated authority {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-attenuation}

When a repair trajectory delegates a subtask to a helper process or transitions from editing `src/pool.py` to running the test suite, handing over the full parent grant lets the helper modify files outside its subtask, while minting an unchecked child grant risks accidentally adding `execute` or `write` rights the parent never held. **Attenuation**\index{Attenuation!definition} prevents privilege escalation during delegation by deriving a child grant that permits no more than its parent. Writing $\GrantAllowedAccesses(\CapabilityGrant)$ for the accesses allowed by a grant, the relation requires

$$
\ChildCapabilityGrant\sqsubseteq \ParentCapabilityGrant
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant).
$$

Narrower object scope, fewer rights, stronger conditions, and an earlier expiry can establish that relation. Consider the repair's edit grant, issued at time $\GrantIssueTime_0$, and two proposed children. All three carry the same condition $\GrantCondition$, which binds use to this task, so the tuples below list only the components that differ:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\EditPhaseCapabilityGrant &= \big(\GrantRights=\{\text{read}, \text{write}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant=\texttt{repo/},\ \GrantExpiryTime=\GrantIssueTime_0 + 300\,\text{s}\big) \\
\TestPhaseCapabilityGrant &= \big(\GrantRights=\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant=\texttt{repo/},\ \GrantExpiryTime=\GrantIssueTime_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{rejected: execute} \notin \EditGrantRights \\
\ScanCapabilityGrant &= \big(\GrantRights=\{\text{read}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant=\texttt{repo/src/pool.py},\ \GrantExpiryTime=\GrantIssueTime_0 + 120\,\text{s}\big) && \text{valid: } \ScanCapabilityGrant \sqsubseteq \EditPhaseCapabilityGrant
\end{aligned}
$$

The test grant fails even though its lifetime is shorter, because it asks for a right the parent never held. Execution needs an appropriate parent grant or a separately authorized grant from the controller. A runtime that intends to support a test phase therefore includes execute in the grant it issues at the start, or issues a new grant for that phase, and then actively withdraws write authority over the source tree when testing begins, which freezes the candidate being graded. Task-local scratch is a separate object in the grant and stays writable, so the tests keep their temporary files. The read-only mount of the acceptance checks is a second layer beneath the grant. Even a grant such as $\EditPhaseCapabilityGrant$ that names all of `repo/` cannot write through that mount. Together the two layers keep a candidate from modifying the fixtures and checks that grade it, the property sealed evaluation depends on.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Sealed evaluation criteria held outside the agent's reach are developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-grader-isolation.
:::

Attenuation can also happen without contacting the issuer. Chained-caveat tokens such as macaroons [@birgisson2014macaroons] let any holder append a restriction and pass on the narrower token. The issuer mints a root token with a message authentication code $\TokenAuthenticationCode_0$ computed under a secret key only it holds. A holder adds caveat $\TokenCaveat_i$ (a path prefix, a rights subset, a turn limit, an earlier expiry) and replaces the code with a keyed hash (HMAC) of the previous code and the caveat,

$$
\TokenAuthenticationCode_i = \text{HMAC}(\TokenAuthenticationCode_{i-1},\, \TokenCaveat_i).
$$ {#eq-vol3-macaroon-chain}

The verifier recomputes the chain of @eq-vol3-macaroon-chain from its root key and admits a request only if every caveat is satisfied. A holder of the child cannot remove a caveat without the prior code $\TokenAuthenticationCode_{i-1}$, which the chain does not reveal, so a subagent or tool worker can narrow authority offline but cannot widen the token it received.

This relation constrains derived authority; a trajectory can still move from inspection to an authorized edit or test phase under explicit policy. Deriving a read-only child also leaves a broader parent that the same holder retained fully usable. If a phase transition is meant to remove write authority, the runtime withdraws or disables the earlier grant and deals with access already opened under it. Delegation must also preserve aggregate budgets: several children together receive at most the parent's resource allowance. Both forms of attenuation share this limit (@fig-vol3-capability-attenuation). A checked derivation narrows what a child may do but leaves the parent usable, and a chained-caveat token narrows what its next holder may do but cannot reach back to restrict a copy of the token someone already holds.

::: {#fig-vol3-capability-attenuation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. Panel A, deriving a grant, lists three grants in rows with columns for rights, objects, and expiry. Each row shows read, write, and execute slots, filled where the right is held. The parent Gamma_edit, marked still usable, holds read and write over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 300 s. A dashed red branch derives Gamma_test, marked rejected, which holds read and a red execute slot over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 120 s. A solid branch derives Gamma_scan, marked valid, which holds read only over repo/src/pool.py with expiry T0 plus 120 s. Expiry bars start from a shared T0 line, the parent bar longer than the child bars. Panel B, appending a caveat, shows an issuer holding key k, two holders, and a verifier. The token grows from id and sigma 0, to id, c1, and sigma 1, to id, c1, c2, and sigma 2, beside the formulas sigma 0 equals HMAC of k and id, sigma 1 equals HMAC of sigma 0 and c1, and sigma 2 equals HMAC of sigma 1 and c2, with c1 a prefix repo/src/ and c2 rights read. The verifier recomputes k to sigma 0 to sigma 1 to sigma 2 and checks every caveat."}
![](images/svg/capability-attenuation.svg)
:::

The operative test is therefore which grants and resource handles the worker can still exercise, rather than merely whether the child grant is narrower. This test applies equally to a helper process inside one trajectory and to a subagent that receives a delegated grant, since passing a grant to another agent leaves the meaning of authority unchanged.

### Expiry and revocation {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-expiry-revocation}

Suppose the repair task's 300-second edit phase expires while a worker process still holds an open writable file descriptor to `src/pool.py`. Rejecting new `open()` calls after $\GrantExpiryTime$ stops fresh handles from being created, but the already-open descriptor continues to permit writes unless the runtime closes the handle or stops the worker. An expiry timestamp states when a grant stops authorizing new use; revoking active access requires an enforcement mechanism that checks status on each operation, closes live handles, and terminates or constrains ongoing processes. When the edit phase ends, the transition must therefore stop or constrain the worker, revoke the usable reference where supported, or move subsequent work into a restricted execution context, and the runtime must record what it has actually confirmed rather than equating a changed policy record with completed revocation.

External effects have their own boundary. A broker can stop accepting new requests after expiry, but a previously admitted remote operation may still complete. A lease or cancellation request does not settle that effect or justify a retry. Environment teardown and readiness for reuse receive their full treatment in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset; here the requirement is that authority have an enforced lifetime rather than an advisory timestamp.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Why an unsettled remote outcome does not justify a blind retry is established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency.
:::

::: {#chk-08-confused-deputy-defense .callout-checkpoint title="Scope, attenuation, and lifetime"}

A repair worker holds read and write access to the candidate source. It derives a read-only grant for `src/pool.py`, retains the original grant, and opens a writable handle before the edit phase expires.

- [ ] **Derived vs. retained grants**: List every reference through which the worker can still write after deriving the child. Which of them must the runtime withdraw to end write authority?
- [ ] **Attenuation test**: A proposed child adds test execution and shortens the expiry. Apply the component-wise check of $\ChildCapabilityGrant \sqsubseteq \ParentCapabilityGrant$ and decide whether it is an attenuation of the edit grant.
- [ ] **Expiry**: When the edit grant expires, the writable handle and one brokered fetch are still open. Decide what the runtime must do with each before it may record revocation as complete.
- [ ] **Test-phase grant**: Write the tuple $(\GrantRights, \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant, \GrantCondition, \GrantExpiryTime)$ for a test phase that keeps writable scratch while the acceptance machinery stays outside the worker's writable scope.

:::

### Credential brokering {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-credential-brokering}

Scoped file and process grants still leave a placement decision for external service secrets: placing a private repository token inside the guest's environment variables or `.netrc` file so the repair worker can run `git fetch` exposes that raw secret to any injected shell command or environment dump that reads process memory or disk. A **credential broker**\index{Credential broker!definition}\index{Credential brokering|see{Credential broker}} instead holds the secret outside the guest and uses it on behalf of an authorized request. For example, when the repair worker requests a fetch from its approved private repository through a host-owned source-service adapter, the broker checks the bound task identity, repository, operation, destination, and current grant, then performs the credentialed request without returning the credential. Permission to fetch does not permit a push or access to another repository, so the worker can cause a narrowly authorized use of the credential without possessing the credential itself.

Brokering requires a supported mediation arrangement. An application adapter can make the upstream request directly; a proxy can attach credentials only where it can legitimately inspect and modify the relevant protocol exchange. A signing service likewise needs to authorize what it signs, not merely conceal its key. @Sec-vol3-sandboxes-egress-enforcement develops how the runtime constrains routes that might bypass these interfaces. If a tool genuinely requires a credential inside the guest, a narrowly scoped, short-lived credential shrinks the scope and window of exposure, while the guest still possesses it for that window.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Tracking whether an allowed request's data may flow to its recipient is developed in @sec-vol3-security-taint-tracking.
:::

Keeping selected credentials outside the guest removes the most valuable target from the README attack, and from the environment dump in the Gemini CLI incident. The environment and repository content remain sensitive, and a brokered operation can still be misused within its permitted scope. Secret placement, access permission, and whether an allowed request's data may flow to its recipient are three distinct concerns: a sandbox governs the first two, where authority resides and how execution is confined to it, whereas the third is an information-flow problem that a sandbox alone cannot settle. Capabilities and brokering specify the resources the runtime intends to expose, and enforcing those limits in practice requires an execution envelope evaluated by what it shares with the host and which components uphold its boundary.

## Choosing an Isolation Envelope {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms}

A lightweight log parser, a multi-turn software repair task compiling code and executing test suites, and an untrusted customer-uploaded binary demand fundamentally different operating interfaces. Selecting an appropriate execution envelope begins with these workload requirements and the host resources that must remain protected, rather than defaulting to a convenient packaging format.

::: {#dfn-isolation-envelope .callout-definition title="Isolation envelope"}

An ***isolation envelope***\index{Isolation envelope!definition} is the enforced boundary around executing code, specified by the resources it exposes, the components it shares with the host or other workloads, and the mechanisms that restrict access and consumption.

1. **Significance**: It makes the permitted reach of an operation a property of its execution environment rather than a request to the model or program.
2. **Distinction**: A grant specifies permitted authority, whereas the envelope enforces that boundary against executing code. Enforcing confinement guarantees that code cannot exceed its assigned reach, but it does not validate whether every permitted operation aligns with the agent's intended task.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating the high-level label of a container, virtual machine, or language runtime as a complete isolation policy without auditing its concrete configuration, host mounts, and exposed system interfaces.

:::

Choosing a different envelope changes both the composition of the trusted computing base defined in the threat model and the interface untrusted code can reach. Narrowing that interface simplifies security review, but counting system calls or source lines cannot produce a quantitative probability of sandbox escape. A systems comparison instead asks which failure modes each envelope contains, which components remain trusted, and which operating interfaces the workload requires. The four envelopes in @fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum differ first in where a system call lands: in the host kernel after a filter, in an emulating user-space kernel, in a separate guest kernel, or nowhere at all, because restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction.

::: {#fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape." fig-alt="Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode stand on one host kernel bar that spans all of them. A dashed horizontal line marked trust boundary crosses every column, with amber untrusted boxes above it and purple trusted boxes below it. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process through a small filter to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call, trapped, to a user-space kernel that emulates the call and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make a native system call to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O crosses the boundary to the monitor with virtual devices, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module with linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports through imported functions only, and the runtime makes host calls for imports."}
![](images/svg/isolation_spectrum_v2.svg)
:::

### Shared and interposed kernels {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-gvisor-vs-microvm}

The first two columns of @fig-vol3-isolation-spectrum start from a standard POSIX process and differ in whether its system calls reach the host kernel directly: when untrusted code issues a permitted system call inside an ordinary container, the host kernel services that call itself, so a single exploitable bug in the shared kernel compromises the entire host. A **shared-kernel container**\index{Shared-kernel container!definition} confines host processes using native operating-system primitives: Linux namespaces restrict views of global resources such as process trees, network interfaces, and mount tables; access controls and seccomp filters restrict permissible operations; and control groups bound resource consumption. Container isolation is therefore only as strong as the host kernel and the configuration around it; packaging an application into an image provides no security boundary on its own.

To avoid exposing the host kernel directly, a **user-space kernel**\index{User-space kernel!definition} places an intermediary kernel implementation between the application and the host operating system. For example, gVisor's Sentry reimplements the Linux kernel API as a memory-safe user-space process written in Go [@google2019gvisor]. The Sentry intercepts application system calls, services them internally without passing the raw call through to the host kernel, and requests host resources through a restricted seccomp filter. An envelope must still be audited by its concrete configuration rather than its name, because the trusted path can change under an unchanged label: gVisor's original design routed every filesystem operation through a separate proxy process so that the Sentry held no host file descriptors, whereas a later revision lets the Sentry open paths itself relative to descriptors handed to it at startup [@gvisor2023directfs]. Because compilers and build tools depend on specific POSIX behaviors, an engineering team must also verify that the user-space kernel supports the system calls its toolchain needs, and pair the emulator with independent storage and compute quotas.

### Separate guest kernels {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-guest-kernels}

When a build or repair task needs full Linux system-call compatibility without exposing the host kernel to guest exploits, user-space emulation can fall short on either coverage or speed. A **microVM**\index{MicroVM!definition} instead runs a real guest kernel and its workload behind a hardware-virtualization boundary\index{Sandbox!hardware virtualization} managed by a virtual machine monitor (VMM). Application system calls execute natively inside the guest kernel, and only interactions with the host cross explicitly configured virtualization and device interfaces. Compromising the guest kernel therefore does not hand control of the host to the attacker; security rests on the monitor, the hypervisor, the CPU virtualization extensions, and the virtual devices exposed to the guest.

Hardware-assisted virtualization roots this isolation directly in processor architectural state [@uhlig2005intel]. The CPU runs the hypervisor in VMX root operation and executes the guest, kernel and applications alike, in VMX non-root operation. Ordinary instructions in non-root operation execute natively, including the guest's own system-call instructions (`syscall` or `sysenter`), which trap into the guest kernel without hypervisor intervention. Sensitive operations,[^fn-sensitive-instruction-trap] such as modifying control registers, reprogramming interrupt controllers, or accessing unmapped physical device registers, trigger a VM exit. During a VM exit, the CPU hardware automatically saves guest register state into the hypervisor-managed Virtual Machine Control Structure (VMCS) and transfers execution control to the hypervisor. Memory translation proceeds through two distinct stages: the guest page tables translate guest virtual addresses to guest physical addresses, and hypervisor-controlled Extended Page Tables (EPT) or Nested Page Tables (NPT)[^fn-nested-page-walk] translate guest physical addresses to host physical memory:

$$
\text{guest virtual} \xrightarrow{\text{guest page tables}} \text{guest physical} \xrightarrow{\text{hypervisor page tables}} \text{host physical}
$$

Even if an untrusted agent exploits a kernel vulnerability inside the guest and gains root privileges, it can rewrite only the first mapping. Because the guest kernel cannot modify the hypervisor's second-stage page tables, it remains physically incapable of addressing host memory frames that the hypervisor has not explicitly mapped into its address space. This hardware boundary is what separates a guest kernel compromise from a host compromise.

[^fn-sensitive-instruction-trap]: **Sensitive Instructions**\index{Virtualization!sensitive instructions}: @popek1974formal stated the classical condition for an efficient virtual machine monitor: every instruction that reads or changes machine control state must trap when run unprivileged, so that the monitor sees it. The x86 architecture had such instructions that did not trap, and hardware extensions added a separate guest mode in which those operations exit to the hypervisor [@uhlig2005intel]. That exit is the enforcement point: guest code cannot change host control state without passing through code the host trusts.

[^fn-nested-page-walk]: **Two-Dimensional Page Walk**\index{Virtualization!nested paging}: On a TLB miss the hardware must translate each guest page-table pointer through the hypervisor's tables as well, so a four-level walk in each dimension can need up to twenty-four memory references instead of four [@bhargava2008accelerating]. Page-walk caches reduce that cost, but a memory-intensive test suite inside a microVM pays more per TLB miss than the same suite in a container. The second mapping that isolates the guest is also a per-miss tax on its memory accesses.

Firecracker\index{Firecracker!microVM isolation} exemplifies this minimalist approach, building on the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) subsystem [@kivity2007kvm]. To minimize both cold-start latency and reachable attack surface, Firecracker originally stripped away legacy PC hardware: it omits a BIOS, dispenses with PCI bus emulation, provides minimal virtio-net and virtio-block devices alongside a basic serial console and minimal keyboard controller, and boots an uncompressed guest kernel directly [@agache2020firecracker]. Subsequent releases introduced ACPI support and an optional virtio-pci transport [@firecracker2025changelog], reiterating that the exposed attack surface depends entirely on the specific version and runtime flags deployed. Furthermore, Firecracker establishes a clean architectural separation: while the VMM exposes virtual network interfaces to the guest, host-side networking infrastructure (such as iptables, nftables, or eBPF programs) enforces outbound egress filtering. The agent's external network policy is thus governed by the host orchestration plane rather than entrusted to the guest [@firecracker2024design].

### Restricted bytecode and host imports {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-wasm}

Not every tool call needs a guest kernel or a POSIX process: a structured log parser that runs for a few milliseconds per call cannot afford even a fast virtual-machine restore on every invocation. A **bytecode sandbox**\index{Bytecode sandbox!definition}[^fn-sfi-origin-sandbox] instead executes code compiled to an intermediate representation whose runtime governs memory accesses and control flow directly. WebAssembly, for example, confines guest code to a contiguous, linear memory space that the runtime isolates using software bounds checks or hardware page-table protections with unmapped guard pages [@haas2017bringing]. WebAssembly defines no native system-call instruction; guest modules interact with the outside world only by calling host functions explicitly imported at instantiation. Those memory boundaries protect the host from the module rather than separating data structures inside the module from one another, and any imported host function runs with host privileges to perform whatever action its implementation allows.

The WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) maps directly to the capability-based security model introduced in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-least-privilege. During module initialization, the host pre-opens specific directory file descriptors and binds them to the sandbox environment. Every subsequent guest path lookup must resolve relative to one of these pre-opened descriptors;[^fn-capsicum-capability-mode] any directory traversal attempting to escape the assigned root (such as `../../etc/passwd`) immediately fails with a capability-violation error before reaching host filesystem primitives.

[^fn-sfi-origin-sandbox]: **Software Fault Isolation**\index{Software fault isolation}: @wahbe1993efficient showed that an untrusted module can be confined to its own region of a shared address space by rewriting its code so that every store and indirect jump is forced into that region, with no hardware protection-domain switch. Bounds-checked linear memory in WebAssembly applies the same confinement to a portable format [@haas2017bringing]. The consequence is the cost row of @tbl-vol3-isolation-transitions: a call into the host is a function call rather than a trap, which is why this envelope suits short per-call tools.

[^fn-capsicum-capability-mode]: **Capability Mode**\index{Capsicum}: Capsicum brought the same discipline to UNIX processes [@watson2010capsicum]. A process in capability mode loses access to global namespaces such as absolute paths and can open files only relative to directory descriptors it already holds, so the descriptors its parent passed in are the whole of its filesystem reach. Preopened handles in a bytecode sandbox and a supervisor's grant installed before `execve` are both ways of handing over the capability before untrusted code starts.
